questions.question: What base model is Llama Guard 3 built on, and what makes it suitable for deployment on mobile hardware?
options: Llama-3.1-70B; quantized to 4-bit reducing memory usage
Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned for content safety; a 1B-INT4 quantized variant runs at over 30 tokens/sec on mobile CPUs
Llama-3.1-8B without fine-tuning; runs natively on mobile GPUs
A custom 3B safety model distilled from Llama-3.1-405B
questions.explanation: Llama Guard 3 is built on Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned for content safety classification. A 1B-INT4 quantized variant runs at over 30 tokens/sec on mobile CPUs, enabling on-device deployment without server infrastructure.

questions.question: What new hazard category does Llama Guard 4 add that is specifically relevant to autonomous coding agents?
options: S13 Elections misinformation
S14 Code Interpreter Abuse
S12 Financial fraud
S15 Autonomous AI behavior
questions.explanation: Llama Guard 4 expands the taxonomy from 13 to S1-S14, adding S14 Code Interpreter Abuse. This category specifically covers autonomous coding agents that execute code in sandboxes, a class of attack the earlier taxonomy did not name.

questions.question: What attack success rate did Emoji Smuggling achieve against six prominent guard systems according to Huang et al.?
options: About 20%
About 50%
About 72%
questions.explanation: Huang et al. (arXiv:2504.11168) showed Emoji Smuggling—inserting non-printable or visually similar emoji between characters of a forbidden request—hit 100% attack success rate on six prominent guard systems. The tokenizer coalesces them differently than the classifier expects.

questions.question: What distinguishes NeMo Guardrails' dialog rails from input and output rails?
options: Dialog rails run on the server while input/output rails run on the client
Dialog rails enforce conversation-level constraints across multiple turns via Colang; input/output rails operate on single turns
Dialog rails are only available for enterprise users while input/output rails are open source
Dialog rails use LLM-based evaluation while input/output rails use rule matching
questions.explanation: Input/output rails classify and block on individual turns. Dialog rails use Colang to define flow constraints that persist across turns—e.g., 'do not discuss medical diagnosis in a customer-support bot even if the user asks three different ways.' This multi-turn awareness is NeMo's key differentiator.

questions.question: Where does the Llama Guard/NeMo classifier layer sit in the full agent safety stack?
options: At the top, as the primary safety mechanism that other layers support
Below the constitutional (model weights) layer and above the runtime layer (permission modes, budgets, kill switches)
At the network layer, filtering requests before they reach the model
At the output layer only, never at the input layer
questions.explanation: The defense-in-depth stack: model weights trained with Constitutional AI provide base refusal behavior, the classifier layer (Llama Guard/NeMo) provides fast reject and category routing, the runtime layer (permission modes, budgets, kill switches) enforces operational limits, and HITL propose-then-commit covers consequential actions.

questions.question: What NeMo Guard Detect attack success rate did Huang et al. measure on jailbreak benchmarks?
options: About 15%
About 35%
questions.explanation: Huang et al. measured 72.54% ASR for NeMo Guard Detect on a jailbreak benchmark under adversarial craft. This is not under casual user conditions—it requires careful attack design—but it demonstrates that classifiers have a ceiling well below 100% coverage even with sophisticated tooling.
